81: The site has to pass three tests: it is visible from the street, it is easy to reach by car, transit or on foot, and it sits near enough guests who match our target profile. Before we sign anything, we confirm with the city that zoning allows a restaurant with a bar at that address. We prefer a second-generation restaurant space, because the venting, grease management and plumbing are already in place, and we budget {{inv_obra}} for the build-out. Rent in the example is {{alquiler_mes}} a month, or {{ocupacion_pct}} of sales, and it is base rent only. If the lease is triple net (NNN), we add property tax, building insurance and common-area charges to that line. We also negotiate renewal options and a cap on annual rent increases, and we ask whether the landlord expects a personal guarantee.
82: The layout serves {{aforo}} seats between the dining room and the bar, and the plan implies about {{rotaciones_dia}} seat turns a day. We give the kitchen enough room for a clean line from prep to the pass, and we keep the walk from the pass to the table short, so food reaches the guest hot. The bar sits where guests see it from the door and where bartenders can serve the bar and the dining room without crossing the kitchen line. Storage, a dish area, staff restrooms and an office complete the plan. A patio adds seats at a lower cost per seat than interior space, but only where the lease and the city permit one. We confirm the permit and any insurance requirement first.
83: Kitchen, Bar and Dining Room Equipment
84: The cooking line is the heart of the kitchen: a range with an oven, a griddle, fryers, a convection oven, refrigerated prep tables, a walk-in cooler and a commercial dishwasher. The plan budgets {{inv_cocina}} for the range and griddle and carries the other pieces as their own startup cost lines. The Type I hood with UL 300 fire suppression is a separate line at {{inv_campana}}. It is usually installed to the NFPA 96 standard for ventilation control and fire protection of commercial cooking, and your fire marshal and mechanical inspector confirm what your city requires. Sinks and a grease interceptor, where the local plumbing code calls for one, have their own line as well. Wherever we can, we buy commercial-grade, NSF-listed equipment, because health inspectors look for it, and we compare quotes for new and used pieces.
85: The bar costs {{inv_barra}} to build and install, and it carries beer taps, a wine refrigerator, an espresso machine and a glass washing station. Dining room tables and chairs come to {{inv_sala}}. We choose durable materials and commercial-grade seating, since furniture takes the most wear in the first years, and we leave room for staff to move without bumping into guests.
87: We split purchasing into three groups: fresh food delivered daily or every other day, beverages delivered weekly, and cleaning and paper goods delivered on a schedule. A broadline distributor covers the basics, and local farms, bakeries and specialty vendors supply the items that set the menu apart. We keep a second supplier for each critical product, so one missed delivery never changes the menu, and we ask distributors about payment terms and volume discounts in writing. In the plan, food costs {{food_cost_comida}} of food sales and beverages cost {{food_cost_bebida}} of beverage sales. Alcohol is bought only from licensed distributors, and we keep invoices for every delivery.
89: Every day starts with a walk-through: we check and log the temperatures of coolers and freezers, count the critical items, review the reservation book, and test the equipment. The kitchen then runs its prep list for the day, with par levels for each station, so that cutting, sauces and bases are ready ahead of service. We plan enough time for prep and a staff meal where the team hears the specials, the 86 list and any allergy notes, and each station is set up before the doors open.
90: Service follows two modes. Guests at the bar expect a drink within a few minutes, while guests at tables expect a first drink and a clear welcome shortly after being seated. Lunch usually turns tables faster than dinner, and we plan staffing around those seat turns rather than around the hours on the door. At close, the bar is counted, the cash drawer is reconciled and documented, perishables are labeled, dated and stored, and the kitchen completes its closing checklist. A manager signs off on each shift.
92: High-turnover items are held at two to three days of par, while dry goods and non-perishables are held longer. We order from the forecast of covers, and a first-in, first-out routine with date labels keeps the walk-in honest. We weigh and record waste daily, so we can see whether a deviation comes from planning, portioning or storage. The bar is counted regularly against sales, because pour costs drift when nobody checks them.
93: The point-of-sale system handles table management, the kitchen display or tickets, reservations and sales reports by item and shift. It also collects sales tax correctly for our location, and it is where we track the average check of {{ticket}} before sales tax. We budget card processing at {{tarjeta_pct}} of sales, plus a software subscription and the hardware, and the startup costs carry the POS and reservation system as their own line.
95: The plan runs two services, lunch and dinner. A general manager opens and closes, a head chef leads the kitchen with line cooks, and servers and bartenders cover the floor and the bar, with part-time servers added for peak hours. A weekend dishwasher and relief shifts keep the schedule honest. We publish schedules in advance and give each shift a clear lead. Full-time schedules stay at {{horas_semana}} hours a week, and we keep time and pay records as the Fair Labor Standards Act requires.
96: Preventive maintenance is part of the operating budget. Refrigeration gaskets and temperatures are checked weekly, the hood and ducts are cleaned on the schedule the fire marshal and the insurer expect, and gas, electrical and fire suppression systems get periodic professional inspections. The grease interceptor is serviced by a licensed hauler on a regular schedule. A small, steady maintenance routine is cheaper than an emergency repair on a Saturday night.
99: A restaurant with a bar of this size needs a core team in place at opening and room to grow once the operation settles. The organization chart has a general manager or owner at the top, who runs the business side, a head chef who owns production and food cost, and a floor lead who owns service in the dining room and at the bar. Below them, line cooks run the kitchen, servers and bartenders handle the guests, part-time servers cover peaks, and a dishwasher supports the kitchen. In the example, the payroll has {{plantilla_puestos}} people, equal to {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents.
100: The general manager or owner combines hospitality skills with control of costs, vendor negotiation and the weekly numbers. In a first restaurant it is common for the owner to work the floor, which lowers fixed costs while the business finds its footing. The head chef needs real line experience, menu development skills, and the habit of costing every plate and ordering to par. We recruit from local networks and from industry boards such as Culinary Agents and Poached, and we test cooks and bartenders with a working interview. Wages in the example sit at or above the legal floor: the federal minimum is $7.25 an hour, about {{salario_minimo_federal}} a year for a full-time position, and many states and cities set a higher minimum that applies instead.
101: We hire in stages. Two months ahead of opening, the head chef and the floor lead join, to build the menu, set up suppliers and design the training. About a week ahead of the opening, the rest of the team arrives, so there is time for a full run of mock services. Between the third and sixth months we look at real sales and seat turns before adding hours. In years 2 and 3 the plan adds a payroll allowance for growth, so promotions and extra servers are budgeted instead of improvised. Employees are hired on a W-2 and paid through payroll, and we avoid treating regular staff as independent contractors.
102: Shifts follow the two services. A day team prepares and serves lunch, and an evening team serves dinner and runs the bar. We schedule from the sales forecast of {{clientes_dia}} covers a day, and the Staffing tab compares the hours we schedule with the hours we need, which gives a coverage of {{cobertura_horas}}. In year 1, labor costs {{personal_a1}} including employer payroll taxes, or {{personal_pct}} of sales. We estimate payroll taxes at {{cargas_pct}} of wages, covering the employer share of Social Security and Medicare, federal and state unemployment taxes and workers' compensation insurance, and your actual rate depends on your state and insurer. Servers and bartenders are budgeted at a full base wage of at least $15 an hour with tips on top, rather than counting on a tip credit.
103: The federal rules for tipped employees are a good example of why this budget is conservative. According to the U.S. Department of Labor, the federal minimum cash wage for tipped employees is $2.13 an hour with a tip credit of up to $5.12, but California, Oregon, Washington, Alaska, Minnesota, Montana and Nevada do not allow a tip credit at all. The workbook does not model tips or a tip credit, so no wage in the plan depends on them. Training starts with two weeks that cover food handling, allergens, the service standards of the house and responsible alcohol service, and it continues with short weekly meetings. We tie a small bonus to guest satisfaction and cost targets, because in a restaurant the people on the floor are the brand.
106: Total startup investment is {{inversion_total}}: {{capex}} for the space, equipment and opening costs, and {{fondo_maniobra}} as a working capital reserve, so the cash we need at opening is {{necesidad_caja}}. The build-out is the largest line at {{inv_obra}}. The cooking line costs {{inv_cocina}}, the Type I hood with UL 300 fire suppression {{inv_campana}}, the bar {{inv_barra}}, dining room tables and chairs {{inv_sala}}, and the liquor license and permits {{inv_licencias}}, an example for a state without a license quota. Launch marketing adds {{inv_lanzamiento}}, and opening inventory adds {{inv_stock}} for the kitchen and {{inv_stock_barra}} for the bar. The Startup Costs tab itemizes every line, including design, legal, technology and contingency, and you replace each figure with your own quotes.
107: The three-year projection starts with year-1 revenue of {{ventas_a1}}, excluding sales tax, built from {{clientes_dia}} covers a day at an average check of {{ticket}} over {{dias}} opening days, which averages {{ventas_dia}} per opening day. Year 2 assumes volume growth of {{crecimiento_a2}} and reaches {{ventas_a2}}, and year 3 adds a further {{crecimiento_a3}} and reaches {{ventas_a3}}. At {{aforo}} seats, the year-1 volume implies {{rotaciones_dia}} seat turns a day. Net profit after income tax at an effective {{impuesto_beneficios}} is {{resultado_neto_a1}} in year 1, {{resultado_neto_a2}} in year 2 and {{resultado_neto_a3}} in year 3, a net margin of {{margen_neto_a1}} in the first year.
108: The cost structure is built from the bottom up. Food costs {{food_cost_comida}} of food sales and beverages cost {{food_cost_bebida}} of beverage sales, which, with packaging and disposables at {{consumibles_pct}}, gives a cost of goods of {{cogs_pct}} and a gross margin of {{margen_bruto_pct}}. Labor is {{personal_pct}} of sales, rent is {{ocupacion_anual}} a year or {{ocupacion_pct}} of sales, marketing is {{marketing_anual}} a year, and card fees are {{tarjeta_pct}}. Prime cost, the sum of food and beverage cost and labor, is the number we watch weekly. According to Restaurant365, a full-service restaurant typically runs 60-65% of sales on prime cost. Total fixed costs in year 1, with depreciation of {{amortizacion_anual}} and interest of {{intereses_a1}}, are {{costes_fijos_a1}}, which leaves EBITDA of {{ebitda_a1}}, or {{ebitda_pct_a1}} of sales.
109: Accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} covers a day, or {{equilibrio_ventas}} of revenue a year, and the plan assumes {{clientes_dia}}. Cash break-even, with loan payments counted and depreciation left out, is {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}} covers a day, or {{equilibrio_caja_ventas}} a year. Our margin of safety over cash break-even is {{holgura_caja_pct}}. Below those levels the restaurant eats into the working capital reserve, which is why we track covers every day from the first week. The lowest cash balance in year 1 is {{saldo_minimo}}, reached in month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}, and you can trace it on the "6. 12-Month Cash Flow" tab.
110: The "4. Scenarios" tab tests demand. In the pessimistic case we serve {{pesimista_clientes}} covers a day at an average check of {{pesimista_ticket}} over {{pesimista_dias}} opening days. Revenue is {{pesimista_ventas}}, the pre-tax result is {{pesimista_resultado}}, and the estimated year-1 closing cash is {{pesimista_caja}}. In the optimistic case we serve {{optimista_clientes}} covers a day at {{optimista_ticket}} over {{optimista_dias}} days, with revenue of {{optimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax result of {{optimista_resultado}}. The base case is the number we ask the lender to underwrite, and the side-by-side view shows how much room we have if the dining room fills more slowly than planned.
111: We fund the project with {{fondos_propios}} of owner equity, or {{aportacion_pct}} of the cash needed, and a {{prestamo}} loan, either a bank loan or an SBA 7(a) loan, at {{tipo_prestamo}} nominal interest (not APR) over {{plazo_prestamo}} years. The annual payment is {{cuota_anual}}, shown as an annual equivalent, because the lender sets the monthly schedule. Lenders usually expect an owner equity injection, so we show it up front. The workbook measures debt service coverage against this loan: year 1 is {{dscr_a1}}, the lowest value over the term is {{dscr_min}}, the workbook warns below {{dscr_limite}}, and a typical lender guideline is {{dscr_objetivo}}. The plan is lender-ready, but approval is never guaranteed.
112: Project payback before debt is {{payback}}, and payback on startup costs alone is {{payback_capex}}. Recovering the capital over several years is normal in restaurants, because a new room needs time to build regulars and to learn its own seasonality. The plan depends above all on controlling food and beverage cost at {{food_cost_comida}} and {{food_cost_bebida}}, keeping labor near {{personal_pct}} of sales, and filling the room at about {{rotaciones_dia}} seat turns a day. Your results will differ, so replace the example numbers in the workbook with your own before you take the plan to a lender.
115: The first step is to understand who regulates what. In the United States the federal government covers things like employer identification numbers, payroll taxes and food labeling rules, the state covers business registration, sales tax, health codes and alcohol, and the county or city covers zoning, building permits, local business licenses and inspections. Requirements vary from one place to the next, so we confirm each item with the local office. The U.S. Small Business Administration notes that you are automatically a sole proprietorship if you do business without registering as anything else, and that an LLC generally protects personal assets such as your house and savings from business liabilities. An LLC is registered with the state, usually through the Secretary of State, and an operating agreement is standard. We also apply for an Employer Identification Number from the IRS, which is free and is needed to hire employees and to pay sales and excise taxes. Talk to an accountant or an attorney about which structure fits you.
116: Next come the health department and the tax registrations. Before construction begins, we submit the layout, equipment list and menu to the local health department for plan review, and after the build-out we pass an inspection to receive the food establishment permit. Rules differ by jurisdiction, so we ask for the checklist in writing. We also register with the state tax agency for a seller's permit or sales tax registration, so we can collect sales tax on food and drinks, and we obtain the business license from the city or county. If we operate under a name other than the legal name, we register a DBA. The SBA's licensing guide explains that the licenses and permits a business needs depend on its activities and location, and it lists restaurants among the regulated activities.
117: Before signing a lease, we confirm with the city that zoning allows a restaurant with a bar at that address, as the SBA recommends for any business that rents or builds a physical space. The build-out then needs building permits and, depending on the scope, electrical, plumbing, mechanical and gas permits, each with its own inspections. Once the space passes its final inspections, the city issues a certificate of occupancy, and we do not open without it. Converting a former restaurant is often faster than finishing a raw shell, but only if the existing permits, venting and grease interceptor still meet current code. Timelines vary widely, so these steps go first on the schedule with a cushion.
118: The kitchen has its own rules. A Type I hood over the cooking line is typically installed with a UL 300 fire suppression system, in line with the NFPA 96 standard for ventilation control and fire protection of commercial cooking operations, and many cities ask for a Class K extinguisher near the fryers. Many cities require a grease interceptor, which the plumbing department reviews, and the fire marshal inspects the hood and suppression system before opening. Each city publishes its own requirements, so we ask early. If we add a patio, the city usually issues a sidewalk café or outdoor seating permit, often seasonal, and may ask for insurance and a layout that keeps walkways clear.
119: The liquor license is the item most likely to set the opening date. Alcohol is licensed by the state, usually through an alcoholic beverage control agency or board, and most places also require local approval. Fees and rules vary enormously: according to WebstaurantStore, a license can cost very little in one county and hundreds of thousands of dollars in another, and in quota states, where the number of licenses is capped, new businesses often have to buy an existing license from a current holder, which can raise the cost sharply. The workbook budgets {{inv_licencias}} for the license and permits as an example for a state without a quota, so replace that figure with your state's real cost. Expect months of processing, and plan for liquor liability insurance, responsible beverage service training for the staff where the state or the insurer expects it, and the required age signage.
120: As an employer, we follow federal and state rules from the first hire: Form I-9 to verify work eligibility, Form W-4 for withholding, state new-hire reporting, required workplace posters and workers' compensation insurance, which almost every state requires. The federal minimum wage is $7.25 an hour according to the Department of Labor, and states and cities may set higher minimums that apply instead. For tipped staff, the federal minimum cash wage is $2.13 an hour with a tip credit of up to $5.12 where the state allows it, and California, Oregon, Washington, Alaska, Minnesota, Montana and Nevada do not. The workbook does not model a tip credit, and servers are budgeted at a base wage of at least $15 an hour.
121: Food safety and insurance close the checklist. Health codes are based on the FDA Food Code, a model code that each state, local or tribal government adopts in its own way. In most places we need a Certified Food Protection Manager, for example through ServSafe, and food handler cards for the rest of the team where required. Federal law recognizes nine major food allergens: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame. We train the team to answer allergy questions and prevent cross-contact, and we print a consumer advisory on the menu for raw or undercooked items where the code calls for it. For insurance we plan on general liability, liquor liability, property coverage and workers' compensation, and the plan budgets {{seguros_anual}} a year, which you should replace with real quotes from an agent who knows restaurants.
122: Allow roughly four to eight months from the first permit application to opening day, and expect the liquor license or the plan review to be the longest wait. Start the applications that depend on each other in order, and keep every approval in a binder at the restaurant. A note for readers in the United Kingdom: alcohol needs a premises licence for the venue and a personal licence for the designated premises supervisor under the Licensing Act 2003, the food business must be registered with the local council at least 28 days before trading, and the council will give a Food Hygiene Rating after inspection (Scotland uses the Food Hygiene Information Scheme). VAT at 20% applies to restaurant sales on the premises, and the 14 allergens must be declared.
125: The American restaurant market keeps rewarding independent operators who offer a clear concept, a warm room and consistent execution. Guests still want to eat out, and they choose more carefully, looking for places with a point of view, fair value and an atmosphere worth the trip. That creates room for a well-defined casual restaurant with a bar, especially in mid-sized cities and growing suburbs where good neighborhood spots have not caught up with demand. We do not lean on a single national growth number. We build the plan from our own volume, check and cost assumptions: {{clientes_dia}} covers a day, an average check of {{ticket}} and {{dias}} opening days a year, which gives {{ventas_a1}} of revenue in year 1 and a gross margin of {{margen_bruto_pct}}.
126: The main risks need a clear plan. Labor is the first one: at {{personal_pct}} of sales in the example, small changes in wages or scheduling move the result. We manage it with versatile staff, schedules built from the sales forecast and a weekly look at coverage, which stands at {{cobertura_horas}} in the model. Food and beverage costs are the second risk, and we answer them with annual supplier agreements, a seasonal menu, daily waste logs and regular bar counts. Competition is the third, and we answer it with a distinct concept and good service. The fourth is liquidity in the early months: the working capital reserve of {{fondo_maniobra}} and a lowest year-1 cash balance of {{saldo_minimo}} give us a cushion, and the pessimistic scenario, with a pre-tax result of {{pesimista_resultado}}, shows what happens if demand falls short.
127: The strengths of the project rest on three pillars: a location chosen on real traffic and visibility, a concept that combines a restaurant kitchen with a bar guests enjoy, and a cost structure designed in the plan from the start. Total startup investment is {{inversion_total}}, funded with {{fondos_propios}} of owner equity and a {{prestamo}} loan. Payback before debt is {{payback}}, accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} covers a day against {{clientes_dia}} planned, and the lowest debt service coverage ratio is {{dscr_min}}, against a typical lender guideline of {{dscr_objetivo}}.
128: The roadmap follows the phases of the opening checklist included with this kit. Phase 1, Business Formation, covers the LLC, the EIN, tax registrations, the bank account and insurance. Phase 2, Location & Permits, covers the site, the lease review, the zoning check and the start of plan review, building permits and the liquor license application. Phase 3, Build-Out & Equipment, covers construction, the hood and fire suppression, the grease interceptor, the cooking line and the bar. Phase 4, Staff, covers hiring and training. Phase 5, Marketing & Launch, covers the Google Business Profile, reservations, social media and the opening campaign. Phase 6, Obligations to Close Before Opening, covers final inspections, the certificate of occupancy, the health permit, the liquor license and posters. Phase 7, First 90 Days, covers a soft opening, feedback and adjustment.
129: We track key indicators every week from day one. The target is {{clientes_dia}} covers a day and {{rotaciones_dia}} seat turns, and the average check, planned at {{ticket}}, tells us whether the bar and the dessert menu are lifting the sale. Sales per opening day, planned at {{ventas_dia}}, show whether we are on plan. Food cost against {{food_cost_comida}}, beverage cost against {{food_cost_bebida}}, labor against {{personal_pct}} of sales and prime cost against the 60-65% benchmark show early whether margins are slipping. We also read new Google and Yelp reviews each month and the share of guests who come back, as signs of satisfaction and word of mouth.
130: Looking three to five years ahead, there are two directions. The conservative path consolidates the first restaurant: stable volume, a trained team, tighter prime cost and a loyal base of regulars, with cash going to repay the loan, which carries an annual payment of {{cuota_anual}}. The expansion path, considered only if the numbers hold, uses the proven concept and documented procedures to open a second room in a complementary neighborhood, funded by the cash the first one generates and by a new lender conversation. We would consider franchising or licensing only if profits are sustained, the operations are fully documented and outside demand is clear.
131: The immediate action plan has four steps. First, decide the investment and the funding mix with your accountant and a lender, using the workbook to test your own numbers. Second, form the company and open the business bank account, so the lease and the permit applications are made in its name. Third, shortlist two or three sites, run the zoning check on each and compare their leases against the occupancy line of {{ocupacion_anual}} a year. Fourth, start the applications with the longest lead times, the plan review and the liquor license, and keep the opening checklist open on the desk. Review the legal items with your local authorities and your accountant, and bring the plan to the bank with confidence.
